chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran, from Abd Allah ibn Sinan, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Nasibi (one who is hostile to the Imams) whose hostility and enmity are known. Can we marry him to a believing woman, when he is able to reject her (or his proposal is rejected), and he does not know of the rejection? He (peace be upon him) said: The believer does not marry the Nasibiyyah, nor does the Nasibi marry the believing woman, nor does the weak one (in religion) marry a believing woman.

key_terms.النَّاصِبَةَ: The hostile woman (female form of Nasibi).
key_terms.النَّاصِبُ: The hostile one (male form of Nasibi).
key_terms.النَّاصِبِ: Nasibi: One who is hostile to the Imams, specifically the Ahl al-Bayt.
key_terms.الْمُسْتَضْعَفُ: The weak one: Refers to one who is weak in faith or religious conviction.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on marrying a Nasibi (hostile to Imams) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the permissibility of intermarriage between believers and the 'Nasibi' (those known for hostility towards the Ahl al-Bayt), specifically addressing the scenario where the believer has the power to reject the union but chooses not to. It establishes that while a believer may marry a Nasibi woman and vice versa, the ruling also extends to the 'Mustad'af' (the weak or doubtful in faith), highlighting the theological significance of marital alliances in preserving communal identity and religious integrity within Shia jurisprudence. The narration underscores that mere knowledge of enmity does not automatically invalidate the marriage contract, provided the believer is capable of managing the relationship.
